_about: Britain's army between home and the Middle East (ruling 229, part 1, with the historian's facts: /mnt/project-files/historian/ruling-229-facts.md, section 1). The grand campaign only, and only for a country the computer runs. 'floor': the field corps its staff keeps at home, from the record. From June 1940 to June 1941 (turns 10 to 22) the Chiefs kept at least twelve divisions in reserve apart from the troops on the beaches, about a third of the field army; from July 1941 to the end of 1942 (turns 23 to 40) about a quarter. The five home commands that hold in place stand for the beach troops and are not counted either way; the field corps are the country's corps that do not hold in place, wherever they stand (the Commonwealth's rows in the desert count among them, as the army the floor is measured against, and never as troops at home). No corps leaves the homeland by sea while its going would leave fewer than 'share' of them at home: not to a landing, not across a narrow sea, not to Egypt. Before turn 10 and after turn 40 no floor is set beyond the five commands. 'reinforce': at the stops of the history dial from 'stop' on, the staff sails its spare field corps from home to the first of the harbours in 'to' its side holds, with room, by the sailing every staff's corps take (one month, as far as the sea lets them), for as long as the theatre's threat outweighs home's. A theatre's threat is the strength of the enemy's corps in or next to the ground its side holds there, joined by land to that harbour; home's is what can really cross the sea to it: the strongest of each enemy's corps in a harbour within a landing's range of its coast, as many as 'waves' months of his shipping carry. Each is weighed against the strength its side stands there with, the threat counted 'cover' times over: a corps sails while the theatre is short and shorter than home. No corps sails over a crossing more dangerous than 'risk', and the sealift caps how many go in a month. 'by' names the seas a sailing to the theatre may cross, and a way that needs any other is not taken (empty: any). Where no harbour at home has a way open to the theatre (with Italy at war the Mediterranean is over 'risk'), the staff sends its spare field corps round the Cape instead, as the War Cabinet did in August 1940 (the design director's b460): under the same weighing, floor and sealift, put to sea from home with no loss on the way (the escorted troop convoys round the Cape lost very little), they land 'cape' months later at the theatre's harbour, or at the nearest its side holds on that front if the enemy has taken it, by the arrival rows' own code. At sea a corps counts in its country's field army, and neither at home nor in the theatre; the staff counts one already at sea for the theatre as on its way. A player's Britain sails as it always has. Stops 1 and 2 keep history's arrival rows alone.
